name: Parana
summary_text: Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework. The state is assessed at the national score: no deviation from the national position has been identified that is material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Curitiba or anywhere else in the state faces the same law as a visitor to any other part of the country.  Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and adoption rights have followed since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Explicit national discrimination protections have rested on that ruling since 2019. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute sits alongside it and that repeal efforts are before Congress.  In 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed nonbinary people to amend their civil records, a document rule that operates in Paraná as elsewhere in Brazil. Intersex people have no specific protections in Brazilian law.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's 2026 overview records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.  Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; placement is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision taken after the person has been consulted about their preference, with female, male and LGBTI-specific units set out and the declared preference recorded. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, documenting housing in units operated as masculine and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.
